title: Where should the cache live — client, CDN, app layer, or DB layer?
summary: Tests whether you can place a cache at the right layer for the specific data instead of defaulting to "we'll add Redis" — client, CDN, app layer, and DB layer each solve a different problem.

slides.markdown:
"Where should the cache live?" expects you to know there are **four distinct layers** — client, CDN, app layer, and database layer — and that each one solves a different problem. The weak answer is "we'll add a Redis cluster" for everything; the strong answer places each piece of data at the layer that actually matches its access pattern.

The interviewer is checking whether "caching" is one tool in your head or four.

Ask: **is this data static assets, personalized data, or a shared computed result?** Static assets (images, JS bundles) belong nowhere near the app server. Personalized data (a session, a per-user feed) can't sit at a shared layer like a CDN without careful scoping. A shared computed result (a product's price, a trending list) is exactly what a distributed app-layer cache is for.

The answer to this question decides the whole rest of your placement — get it wrong and every later answer follows the wrong path.

Match the layer to the data: **static → CDN or client cache. Shared computed results → an app-layer distributed cache** (Redis, Memcached). **Per-row lookups → the database's own buffer cache** or a read replica.

The underlying logic: each layer is closest to a different kind of access pattern. The CDN sits closest to the user and is great at serving the same bytes to everyone; the app-layer cache sits closest to your business logic and is great at avoiding repeated computation; the DB layer is closest to the data itself and is great at avoiding repeated disk reads for the same row.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: one product page, three cache layers
slides.markdown:
![One product page's images, price, and inventory routed to three different cache layers](assets/product-page-cache-layers.svg)

A single product page load can touch all three layers at once: the **images** come from the CDN, the **price** comes from an app-layer cache (computed from currency/discount rules, shared across users), and the **inventory count** is read straight from the database because it needs to be current.

Naming which field goes to which layer, on one concrete page, is the strongest way to show you understand placement rather than reciting the four layers abstractly.

slides.sectionTitle: The same data cached at two layers at once
slides.markdown:
Layers stack, and often the same byte is cached twice on its way to the user: a **browser cache** sits in front of a **CDN**, which sits in front of an **app-layer cache**, which sits in front of the database. A repeat visitor's browser might never even ask the CDN; a first-time visitor's CDN edge node might never ask the app layer.

This isn't redundancy for its own sake — each layer is cheaper and faster than the one behind it, so a hit at any layer saves the cost of every layer behind it. The trade-off is that now a piece of data can be stale in multiple places at once when it changes.

slides.sectionTitle: Worked example: a session token vs a static logo, same page load
slides.markdown:
On the very same page load, a **session token** is cached at the app layer (in Redis, keyed per user, never shared) while the **site logo** is cached at the CDN (one file, shared across every user on the planet). Putting the session token at the CDN would leak one user's session toward another; putting the logo at the app layer would waste a distributed cache's capacity on something that never varies per request.

The test isn't naming the four layers — it's picking the right one per piece of data on the same page, in the same breath.

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud
slides.markdown:
| Layer | Latency win | Invalidation difficulty |
|---|---|---|
| Client/browser | Largest — zero network hop | Hardest — you can't reach into a user's browser |
| CDN | Large — one regional hop | Hard — purge APIs, but propagation isn't instant |
| App layer | Moderate — one datacenter hop | Easier — you control the cache directly |
| DB layer | Smallest — still a query | Easiest — tied to the write path itself |

**How to decide:** caching closer to the user cuts latency the most but makes invalidation progressively harder — pick the closest layer you can still reliably invalidate for this data's freshness requirement.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: "what changes if the user base is global?"
slides.markdown:
Going global pushes you toward **edge caching and regional cache tiers**: a CDN with points of presence near each user region, and — for the app layer — regional cache clusters rather than one central one, so a request from Singapore doesn't round-trip to a cache in Virginia.

This also reopens the invalidation question at a bigger scale: purging a key now means purging it across every region, and a write in one region can leave stale reads in another until that propagation completes. Naming this explicitly is what separates "we'd use a CDN" from an answer that scales.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: "how do you know which layer served a stale response?"
slides.markdown:
With four layers stacked, a stale response could have come from any of them, and debugging "why is this user seeing old data" gets much harder without a plan. The practical answer: **tag the response with which layer served it** — a cache-status header or log field at each hop (client, CDN, app, DB) — so a support ticket can be traced back to the exact layer holding the stale copy.

Without this, you're stuck manually checking browser dev tools, CDN dashboards, and Redis TTLs one by one every time someone reports stale data.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: one Redis cluster for everything
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "We need caching, so let's stand up one Redis cluster and put everything in it — sessions, static config, computed prices, rate-limit counters."

**Why it's wrong:** it ignores that static assets belong at the CDN (cheaper, closer to the user, and the app-layer cache shouldn't pay for serving images), and it concentrates unrelated access patterns — a hot rate-limit counter and a rarely-read config blob — onto one cluster's capacity and eviction policy, so one workload's churn can evict another's hot keys.

**Correct model:** pick the layer per data type first, and treat "one Redis cluster" as the answer only for the subset of data that genuinely belongs at the app layer.

Four layers, four jobs: client/CDN for static and shared content, app layer for computed and shared results, DB layer for repeated row reads. Match the layer to the access pattern, not to a default tool. The closer to the user, the bigger the latency win and the harder the invalidation — name that trade-off explicitly. Going global means edge tiers and regional invalidation; debugging staleness across layers means tagging which layer served each response.
